newsitem.title: USA: Socialism alive and well in Vermont.
newsitem.headline: Socialism alive and well in Vermont.

text.p: Socialism may be dying elsewhere in the world but it is alive and well in Vermont, where it even has Democratic Party backing.
Bernie Sanders, the only Socialist in Congress, has the support of both the state and national Democratic parties, angering the only Democrat in the race, Jack Long.

"I'm very angry and I don't know what to do about it," said Long, 52, a former state environmental commissioner under Democratic Gov. Howard Dean. He calls himself "a moderate, reasonable Democrat" and says Sanders is "too radical."
Sanders declined to be interviewed for this article.

Just before announcing his candidacy for Sanders' House seat, Long said, he received a phone call from Robert Engel, executive director of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, telling him not to run. When Long refused, he said, Engel told him, "If there is a way I can hurt you, I will."

Consequently, Long has received no funding from the DCCC for his race and instead has seen Democrats like White House Senior Adviser George Stephanopoulos campaign for Sanders. "There is a very liberal element in the White House," Long said. "And frankly, they don't have to spend any money to have Bernie's votes."
It was not the first time Democrats decided against challenging Sanders. They did not oppose him in 1994.

The latest poll shows both Long and Republican state Sen. Susan Sweetser far behind Sanders. The Becker Institute survey of 400 registered voters found Sanders with 52 percent, Sweetser with 33 percent and Long with 5 percent. The poll conducted during the second week of October has a five percentage point margin of error.

Sanders, son of a Brooklyn paint salesman, came to Vermont as part of the hippie invasion in 1968 and won his first political office by 10 votes when he was elected mayor of Burlington. Since he was first elected to the House as Vermont's only representative, he has usually voted with the Democrats. He heads the congressional progessive caucus, which consists of him and 55 Democrats, according to his campaign.

Usually tieless, rumpled and seen as sincere, Sanders criticises liberals because they are too far to the right. He has supported a Canadian-style single-payer health care plan and creation of a national cancer registry to collect data on environmental causes of cancer, has been a consistent critic of the Republican Contract With America and regularly calls for major cuts in military spending.
But to the consternation of his liberal supporters, he voted against the Brady gun control bill, saying it was "tokenism" and "pure symbolism" and handgun control should not be a federal conern.

This year, he has accepted contributions from the National Rifle Association for his more than $700,000 campaign war chest. The NRA worked to defeat Sander's predecessor, Peter Smith, who had voted to ban semiautomatic weapons.

And in this state of 600,000 people near the Canadian border, Sanders opposed the North American Free Trade Agreement. "NAFTA has been a disaster," he said recently. "Before NAFTA we had a trade surplus with Mexico. In 1995, after NAFTA, the United States compiled a $15.4 billion trade deficit with Mexico. This equates to the loss of over 260,000 American jobs."

But Democrat Long argued, "For Vermont, NAFTA is an economy booster and job creator." He estimated the state would gain 950 jobs next year as a direct result of trade with Mexico. Republican Sweetser also favours NAFTA.

Sweetser has seen a parade of prominent Republicans stump for her including New York Representative Susan Molinari and Representative John Kasich of Ohio, head of the House Budget Committee, and has amassed a $445,000 campaign fund.
